Patient educationArticle writing

Making an unfamiliar appointment feel less daunting.

A patient guide that starts with the emotional reality of an examination, then turns preparation into a sequence of manageable steps.

Read the original sampleExplore the writing
FROM THE SAMPLE
“Let them know how you’re feeling during the examination”

A direct invitation to speak up.

Inside the piece Context, structure & a reading preview

How do I prepare for a gynaecological examination?

Reader focus
Someone preparing for a gynaecological examination who wants to know what to expect.
Content structure
Acknowledges anxiety first, then moves through appointment planning, useful information to bring, and communicating with the clinician.
Editorial observation
The closing passage returns agency to the reader. Reassurance is part of the structure, rather than a reassuring sentence added at the end.

Before you open the document

The guide opens by naming anxiety and uncertainty. It then organizes preparation around what happens before the appointment and what information the reader may need. The final note encourages communication with the healthcare provider.

Reproductive healthArticle writing

Connecting reproductive health to everyday life.

A long-form explainer that connects a complex subject with familiar routines, using an accessible metaphor to give the reader a way in.

Read the original sampleExplore the writing
FROM THE SAMPLE
“Think of your body as the garden where a potential pregnancy will take root.”

An everyday image introduces an unfamiliar topic.

Inside the piece Context, structure & a reading preview

Lifestyle habits that affect fertility

Reader focus
A general reader exploring the relationship between lifestyle and reproductive health.
Content structure
Moves from nutrition and body weight to substances, stress, sleep, and exercise, grouping a broad topic into recognizable everyday themes.
Editorial observation
A garden metaphor introduces the topic. The conclusion shifts away from an all-at-once overhaul toward gradual change, giving the piece a gentler landing.

Before you open the document

The article uses everyday habits as its organizing thread. It opens with a garden metaphor, explores several lifestyle themes, and closes by encouraging gradual change rather than an abrupt overhaul.

Health awarenessArticle writing

Turning a broad health question into a clear reading path.

An educational article organized around a question a reader might actually ask, with descriptive sections that make a wide topic easier to scan.

Read the original sampleExplore the writing
FROM THE SAMPLE
“it’s important to consult a healthcare professional.”

The next step points toward professional care.

Inside the piece Context, structure & a reading preview

How do you know if you have diabetes?

Reader focus
A non-specialist reader looking for an introduction to diabetes and when to seek professional advice.
Content structure
Introduces the topic, distinguishes types, and separates signs, risk factors, and management into sections with numbered or bulleted information.
Editorial observation
Plain-language explanations sit beside technical terms, while the article directs readers toward professional consultation instead of presenting a diagnosis.

Before you open the document

The sample introduces diabetes before moving through types, symptoms, risk factors, and management. Lists make the material easier to scan, and the article includes a clear prompt to consult a healthcare professional.

Thinking beyond a single article.

A small example of how related reader questions can form a useful content series.

Independent portfolio exercise · Proposed content plan

A first-visit content series for a women’s health practice.

A concept for a hypothetical practice, built around the patient-education topics in this portfolio.

Audience
People approaching an unfamiliar appointment and looking for clear, reassuring information.
Content objective
Help readers move from “What will happen?” to “What should I ask?”
Understand

What happens at a first visit?

An introductory explainer that answers common questions before discussing preparation.

Prepare

How can I feel ready?

A practical preparation guide, linked from appointment information.

Participate

What do I want to ask?

A short question checklist that supports a conversation with the clinician.

See the editorial and measurement plan

Editorial approach: Use the patient’s question as the headline. Put the direct answer first, explain unfamiliar terms, and end with the next useful action. Have medical guidance reviewed by a qualified clinician before publication.

Distribution: Connect the articles as a series on the practice’s website; adapt the preparation checklist for appointment emails.

What to evaluate: Search queries that bring readers to each guide, engagement with related articles, and feedback about unanswered appointment questions. Establish a baseline before setting targets.

Proposed evaluation criteria for this independent exercise.

Good writing has a reason.

Here’s how I think about the work.

Understand before writing.

Start with the reader, the questions they’re asking, and what the content needs to do.

Give every idea a place.

Shape a clear direction, useful themes, and a structure that makes the message easy to follow.

Make every word earn it.

Turn the thinking into accessible, empathetic writing. Then edit for clarity, flow, and purpose.

S.

Clarity is a form of care.

I’m Sophiat Ismail. I write about health, wellness, and the everyday choices that shape our lives.

I’m drawn to the space between complex information and the person who needs to understand it. That’s where clear language, thoughtful structure, and a little empathy can make a real difference.

The goal is simple: make the reader feel informed, not overwhelmed.
